newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Chechen president pledges peace, independence.
newsitem.headline: New Chechen president pledges peace, independence.

text.p: Chechnya's first post-war president Aslan Maskhadov took office on Wednesday, pledging to realise the dream of independence for which his ancestors and contemporaries fought Russia.

Maskhadov, a former Soviet artillery colonel who led separatist rebels against Russian troops sent to crush them in December 1994, also promised to strengthen the Moslem religion and fight a crime wave in the shattered region.

"Now it's the duty of each and every one of us to realise the expectations of our ancestors, our heros fallen in the holy war, of the right to live freely and independently," Maskhadov told rebels and Russian representatives in the Chechen capital.

"For hundreds of years our nation was not allowed to live freely, to be master of its country. Killed when they wanted to kill, burned when they felt like it, labelled 'bandits' when they felt like it, deported when they felt like it."

The soft-spoken Maskhadov, who spent the 21-month conflict with Russia in military fatigues, wore a dark suit and a traditional astrakhan fur hat for the ceremony, held in a suburb of Grozny whose centre was flattened in the war.

Behind him on the stage of the suburban assembly hall stood leaders of the rebel force which humiliated the Russian military in fighting which killed tens of thousands of people and left many more homeless.
Alexander Lebed, former security adviser to President Boris Yeltsin, sat in the audience as did Ivan Rybkin, current secretary of Russia's Security Council.

Lebed signed a peace deal with Maskhadov in August, agreeing to pull out troops and bringing fighting to an end. The Chechens, conquered by Tsarist forces over a century ago and sent en masse into internal exile in Central Asia by dictator Josef Stalin during World War Two, now seek full independence.

But Moscow, fearing separatism elsewhere on its vast territories, insists the region is a part of the Russian Federation and will not discuss sovereignty for five years. Foreign governments, unwilling to anger the Kremlin, would also balk at diplomatic recognition.

Tim Guldimann, the Swiss diplomat and peace broker expelled from Chechnya by outgoing President Zemlikhan Yandarbiyev soon after Maskhadov was elected, was also there. "I'm back!" he told Reuters with a big grin.

Yandarbiyev ejected Guldimann, head of the Chechnya mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, for his position that Chechnya was part of Russia, but the former Chechen leader later softened his stance.

Shamil Basayev, Russia's enemy number one who led a hostage raid inside Russia in 1995 and then stood against Maskhadov and Yandarbiyev in the January poll, turned up at the ceremony just as Maskhadov began to speak.
Security was extremely tight, with hundreds of armed men packing the hall and others crowded on the street outside.
"In the name of the prophet born in Mecca I swear to be an honest servant of the people and a slave of Allah," Maskhadov said in his oath of office.
"Comrades-in-arms I thank you for your goodness...with which you have held out this war. We, brothers in faith and in arms, have won and may Allah let us stick to our path."
When he had finished a deafening roar broke out as hundreds of men fired their Kalashnikov rifles into the air, shooting, filling the air with the smell of gunpowder.
Maskhadov promised to bring the myriad armed groups in the region into line and to protect Chechnya's Russian population.

"First of all it's necessary to strengthen the Moslem religion, to free the nation from the violence and mockery of criminal elements. To that I will direct all my efforts. A state cannot consider itself free whose citizens are in constant fear of their lives," he said.
